newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: LABOR SEETHING OVER IR DEAL
An agreement between the Federal Government and the Democrats guaranteeing the Workplace Relations Bill passage through the Senate has been described as "tawdry" by Labor.
The ALP says the Democrats have won precious little for workers in the compromise, leaving Labor the only party representing workers.
However, Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says input from the Democrats has improved the bill, and the deal's left Labor marginalised.
Democrats leader, Cheryl Kernot, says she's sure safeguards built into the bill by her party will better protect workers, and has accused Labor of being hypocritical.
Neither the Government, nor the Democrats, are ruling out further changes, and Labor and the Greens are expected to suggest further amendments.
The Government's hopeful debate on the bill will begin this week.
EUTHANASIA DEBATE CONTINUES TODAY
The euthanasia question arises again today, with the bill designed to override the Northern Territory's euthanasia legislation, due to be debated in the Federal Chamber.
The Northern Territory's sole Federal Member Nick Dondas says he'll underline Territory rights in his speech on the anti-voluntary euthanasia bill.
Mr Dondas will be one of six speakers in the debate which will last 90 minutes before being moved to a side chamber.
He says it's unthinkable one parliament would override a decision of another parliament.
CONDEMNATION OF INDEPENDENT MP GROWS
The Northern Territory's Member for Greatorex is one of five Australian parliamentarians of Chinese descent to issue a joint statement condemning Independent Queensland MP Pauline Hanson.
Richard Lim says Ms Hanson's anti-Asian comments are unhelpful, and she should desist.
He says the debate on immigration and race is causing angst in multicultural Australia.
Mr Lim says immigrants of Asian descent are Australians too, and make a contribution to Australian society.
DAY TWO OF SOLAR CHALLENGE GETS UNDERWAY
The cars in the world solar challenge begin their second day of racing soon.
They're spread over hundreds of kilometres of the Stuart Highway in the Northern Territory, with the Honda Dream well ahead after a first-day record distance of 774 kilometres.
It'll resume its journey this morning from about 40 kilometres south of Elliott.
The Swiss Schooler entry is more than 60 kilometres back in second place.
The Honda team, whose car averaged 92 kilometres an hour yesterday, says it'll try to break the world record of eight-hundred-and-20 kilometres in a single day, either today or tomorrow.
TESTS ON SUSPECT DRINKING WATER
Investigations have begun into reports that septic overflows are emptying into Sydney's drinking water from the southern highlands.
A land owner near Cambden has tested water at Werriberri Creek, which runs into Warangamba Dam, and found levels of toxic bacteria much higher than accepted limits.
Wollondilly Council manager Gary Clarke says council might stop access to the creek if an independent analysis confirms the high pollution readings.
CALLS FOR UNITED STANCE ON EARLY CHILDHOOD POLICIES
An expert in early childhood has told an industry conference in Newcastle that different childcare sectors need to put aside their differences in light of federal budget cuts.

Dr Gail Halliwell, from the Queensland University of Technology's centre for applied studies in early childhood says as the number of earlier childhood educational services has grown, so has the bickering between them.
She says in 1994, there were 340 different organisations nationwide, and many parents are now confused as to exactly what services each organisation provides.
KEATING RETURNS TO JAKARTA
Former Prime Minister Paul Keating today makes his first visit to the Indonesian capital Jakarta since losing office.
As Prime Minister Mr Keating visited Jakarta six times and developed close ties with Indonesia's long serving president Suharto.
He'll be addressing a major financial conference and is expected to meet a number of key Indonesian leaders.

Last week Foreign Minister Alexander Downer blamed remarks made by Mr Keating during the last election campaign for continuing doubts in Asia about the new Coalition government commitment to the region.
So far Paul Keating has refused to respond to Mr. Downer's accusation.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
